evidence_items.claim: Ancient background for Divine Mercy includes covenant life, temple worship, royal ideology, wisdom teaching, and early church confession; the entry ties that world to Exodus 34:6-7, Psalm 103:8-13, mercy-theme, and grace without letting comparison replace the biblical witness.
Divine Mercy is read across the canon as Scripture develops this theme from Israel's story into the New Testament witness.

Ancient background for Grace includes covenant life, temple worship, royal ideology, wisdom teaching, and early church confession; the entry ties that world to Exodus 34:6-7, Psalm 103:8-13, mercy-theme, and divine-mercy without letting comparison replace the biblical witness.
Grace is read across the canon as Scripture develops this theme from Israel's story into the New Testament witness.

Ancient background for Mercy Theme includes covenant practice, worship, kingship, wisdom instruction, and prophetic critique; the entry ties that world to Exodus 34:6-7, Psalm 103:8-13, divine-mercy, and grace without letting comparison replace the biblical witness.
Mercy Theme is read across the canon as Scripture develops this theme from Israel's story into the New Testament witness.
Responsible contemporary use must distinguish biblical wording, epistolary voice, historical reconstruction, lexical claims, doctrine, reception, pastoral judgment, and modern analogy.
Epiphaneia language joins salvation's manifestation with expectation of the glory of the great God and Savior Jesus Christ.
Titus is told to present himself as an example of good works, integrity, dignity, and sound speech.
Grace is portrayed as having appeared for salvation and as training people for self-controlled, just, and godly life while they await hope.
Titus 2 addresses older men, older women, younger women, younger men, Titus, and enslaved people through differentiated ethical instruction.
Instruction to younger women reflects ancient household reputation and labor conventions rather than a complete timeless definition of women's vocation.
Older women are instructed to teach what is good and to train younger women.
Papyrus 32 preserves parts of Titus 1:11-15 and 2:3-8 and is commonly dated around 200 CE.
Christ's self-giving is connected to redemption from lawlessness, purification of a special people, and zeal for good works.
The letter instructs enslaved people to submit, avoid contradiction and misappropriation, and display trustworthiness without abolishing the slaveholding institution.
The surviving Codex Vaticanus ends before the Pastoral Epistles and is not a manuscript witness to Titus.
Sound teaching is portrayed as embodied conduct among differentiated groups, not merely assent to propositions or conformity to a single later confessional system.
Older women are explicitly represented as teachers of what is good; reception that universally silences women's teaching must account for this positive role.
Gender and household instruction reflects ancient household convention; it does not by itself prescribe one modern household economy, exclude paid work, or authorize misogyny and coercive submission.
Anti-LGBTQ coercion cannot be derived from Titus's age- and gender-group teaching; modern identities and coercive policies are not lexical equivalents of its household terms.
Titus's example is constrained by integrity, dignity, and sound speech; it does not create leader infallibility, clerical caste, or freedom from safeguarding and correction.
Slavery: Titus addresses enslaved people inside an exploitative Roman institution and does not command enslavers to abolish it; this must be named before rejecting slavery apologetics.
Slavery reception: submission and adornment language cannot justify slavery apologetics, trafficking, worker exploitation, abuse concealment, or demanding compliance from people in danger.
Grace is personified as appearing and training people to reject destructive desire and live justly and godly while awaiting hope.

Epiphaneia can describe manifestation or appearing; whether 2:13 grammatically identifies Jesus as 'our great God and Savior' and how it relates to 2:11 and later doctrine receives detailed syntactic discussion.
Christ's self-giving is directed toward redemption, purification, and a people zealous for good works; it cannot be used to glorify abuse, coerced sacrifice, or prosperity extraction.
A 'special' or 'treasured' people echoes scriptural peoplehood language; Christian reception must not turn this into supersessionism, ethnic superiority, or nationalism.
Good works are repeatedly required as the fruit and public form of grace, not identified as the basis that earns divine mercy.
Manuscripts: P32 preserves only Titus 1:11-15 and 2:3-8; Sinaiticus and later witnesses extend coverage, while surviving Vaticanus does not contain Titus.

Application: Titus must not be used for antisemitism, supersessionism, anti-Cretan contempt, misogyny, anti-LGBTQ coercion, authoritarian office, slavery apologetics, nationalism, colonial mission, forced conversion, prosperity extraction, public shaming, or ecological neglect.
